questions.stem: Which structural feature must a monomer have to undergo addition polymerisation?
options: A hydroxyl group at each end
A ring of six carbon atoms
questions.explanation: In addition polymerisation the C=C double bond opens and the monomers join end to end. Two reactive groups, such as -OH and -COOH, are what a condensation polymer needs.

questions.stem: Which monomer is used to make polyethene?
questions.explanation: Polyethene is made by addition polymerisation of ethene. Ethane has no double bond, so it cannot add to other molecules.

questions.stem: What is the monomer of polytetrafluoroethene (PTFE)?
questions.explanation: Tetrafluoroethene has four fluorine atoms on a C=C bond. When it polymerises, every carbon in the chain carries two fluorine atoms, -CF₂-CF₂-. CF₃-CF₃ has no double bond, so it cannot polymerise by addition.

questions.stem: Propene, CH₂=CHCH₃, undergoes addition polymerisation. Which is the repeating unit of the polymer?
questions.explanation: Only the two carbons of the double bond become part of the chain; the CH₃ group hangs off as a side group. A straight -CH₂-CH₂-CH₂- chain wrongly puts the methyl carbon in the backbone, and the chain in an addition polymer has no double bonds.

questions.stem: Part of a polymer chain is -CH₂-CHCl-CH₂-CHCl-CH₂-CHCl-. Which monomer was used?
questions.explanation: The repeating unit is -CH₂-CHCl-, two carbons long, with one Cl on alternate carbons. Putting the double bond back between those two carbons gives chloroethene, CH₂=CHCl.

questions.stem: Which is the repeating unit of the polymer made from but-2-ene, CH₃CH=CHCH₃?
questions.explanation: The double bond is between carbons 2 and 3, so those two carbons form the backbone and each carries a methyl side group. -CH₂-CH(CH₂CH₃)- is the repeating unit from but-1-ene.

questions.stem: Which statement correctly describes the process of addition polymerisation?
options: The monomers join through their functional groups, which become ester links
No by-product forms, so the polymer has the same empirical formula as the monomer
Water is released at each link, so the polymer has fewer atoms than its monomers
Two different monomers are always needed, one at each end of each repeating unit
questions.explanation: All the atoms of the monomers end up in the polymer, so polyethene and ethene are both CH₂ in empirical formula. Losing water and forming ester links describes condensation polymerisation.

questions.stem: A molecule of polyethene has a molar mass of about 56 000 g mol⁻¹. About how many ethene units (M = 28.05 g mol⁻¹) does it contain?
questions.explanation: Number of units = 56 000 / 28.05 ≈ 2000. Because no atoms are lost in addition polymerisation, each repeating unit has the same mass as one ethene molecule.

questions.stem: Which feature is characteristic of condensation polymerisation but not of addition polymerisation?
options: The monomers must each contain at least one carbon-carbon double bond
The polymer has the same empirical formula as its monomer
Only one type of monomer can ever be used to make the polymer
A small molecule, such as water, is released as each link forms
questions.explanation: In condensation polymerisation, functional groups on the monomers react and eliminate a small molecule, usually water. The double bond and identical empirical formula belong to addition polymers.

questions.stem: Which pair of monomers can react to form a polyester?
options: Two alkenes with different side groups
A diol and a dicarboxylic acid
A diamine and a dicarboxylic acid
An alcohol and a monocarboxylic acid
questions.explanation: Each diol molecule can form ester links at both ends, and so can each diacid, so the chain can keep growing. A single alcohol and a monocarboxylic acid give only one small ester molecule, and a diamine with a diacid gives a polyamide.

questions.stem: Which linkage joins the monomer units in nylon?
questions.explanation: Nylon is a polyamide: the carboxylic acid groups react with amine groups, losing water and forming amide links. An ester link is found in polyesters such as PET.

questions.stem: Nylon-6,6 is made from two monomers, each with six carbon atoms. Which are they?
questions.explanation: A polyamide needs amine groups at both ends of one monomer and carboxylic acid groups at both ends of the other. A diol with a diacid would give a polyester, not a nylon.

questions.stem: Polyethylene terephthalate (PET) is a polyester. Which pair of monomers is used to make it?
questions.explanation: PET forms when the -OH groups of ethane-1,2-diol react with the -COOH groups of benzene-1,4-dicarboxylic acid (terephthalic acid), forming ester links. A diamine would form amide links, and ethene polymerises by addition.

questions.stem: Part of a polymer chain is -O-CH₂CH₂-O-CO-CH₂CH₂-CO-O-CH₂CH₂-O-CO-. Which monomers were used?
questions.explanation: Splitting each ester link and adding back water gives HO-CH₂CH₂-OH and HOOC-CH₂CH₂-COOH. The acid has four carbons including both carboxyl carbons, so it is butanedioic acid.

questions.stem: 100 molecules of a diol react with 100 molecules of a dicarboxylic acid to form a single linear polyester chain. How many water molecules are released?
questions.explanation: Joining 200 monomers in a line needs 199 links, and each ester link releases one water molecule. The ends of the chain still carry a free -OH and a free -COOH.

questions.stem: Which single compound could form a condensation polymer by reacting with itself?
questions.explanation: A molecule with an -OH at one end and a -COOH at the other can form ester links at both ends, building a chain. Ethanol and ethanoic acid each have only one reactive group, and ethene polymerises by addition, not condensation.

questions.stem: High-density polyethene is more rigid and melts at a higher temperature than low-density polyethene. Why?
options: Its chains are heavily branched, so they tangle and are held by covalent cross-links
Its chains contain polar groups, so they hydrogen bond strongly to each other
Its chains are joined by ionic bonds, so much more energy is needed to separate them
Its chains have little branching, so they pack closely and dispersion forces are stronger
questions.explanation: Unbranched chains can line up and pack closely, increasing the contact between chains and so the dispersion forces. Branched LDPE chains cannot pack as well. Polyethene has no polar groups, so there is no hydrogen bonding.

questions.stem: How does increasing the average chain length of a polymer such as polyethene affect its properties?
options: Melting point and strength increase, as dispersion forces between chains increase
Melting point and strength decrease, as longer chains have more weak points in them
Melting point rises because covalent bonds now form between neighbouring chains
Melting point stays the same because the chains are made of the same repeating unit
questions.explanation: Longer chains have more surface in contact with neighbouring chains and become more tangled, so the total dispersion forces are larger and more energy is needed to separate them. No covalent bonds form between chains simply because they are longer.

questions.stem: A plastic has covalent cross-links between its chains. How does this affect its behaviour on heating?
options: It melts sharply at one temperature, like a pure molecular solid
It becomes a better conductor of electricity as it is heated
It does not soften or melt, but decomposes at high temperature
It softens at a low temperature and can be remoulded many times
questions.explanation: Covalent cross-links hold the chains in a rigid network, so they cannot slide past each other. Heating eventually breaks covalent bonds and the plastic decomposes rather than melting. Plastics without cross-links soften and can be remoulded.

questions.stem: PTFE is used as the non-stick coating on frying pans. Which feature of its structure explains this use?
options: Hydrogen bonds between its chains make it very hard and resistant to scratching
Cross-links between its chains make it conduct heat well from the pan to the food
Polar C-F bonds make its surface attract water, so food slides off the coating
Strong C-F bonds and a sheath of fluorine atoms make it unreactive and non-stick
questions.explanation: The C-F bond is very strong and the fluorine atoms surround the carbon chain, so PTFE resists heat and chemicals and has very weak attractions to other substances. PTFE has no hydrogen bonding, and its chains are not cross-linked.

questions.stem: Nylon is used for strong fibres such as ropes. Which interaction between neighbouring nylon chains most explains its strength?
options: Hydrogen bonds between N-H and C=O groups of the amide links
Covalent cross-links between the carbon atoms of adjacent chains
Ionic attractions between charged amine and carboxylate ends
Hydrogen bonds between C-H groups and oxygen atoms of the chains
questions.explanation: The amide links of one chain line up with those of the next, so the N-H of one forms hydrogen bonds with the C=O of another. Nylon is not cross-linked, and C-H bonds are not polar enough to hydrogen bond.

questions.stem: PET has polar ester groups in its chains but no O-H or N-H groups in the repeating unit. Which intermolecular forces act between PET chains?
options: Dispersion forces alone, as PET is non-polar
questions.explanation: Every chain has dispersion forces, and the polar C=O and C-O bonds of the ester groups add dipole-dipole forces. With no H bonded to N or O in the repeating unit, the chains cannot hydrogen bond to each other.

questions.stem: Which describes the general structure of an α-amino acid?
options: An amino group and a hydroxyl group bonded to the same carbon, along with H and a side chain R
An amide group bonded to a carbon that also carries a side chain R and a carboxyl group
An amino group and a carboxyl group bonded to the same carbon, along with H and a side chain R
An amino group at one end of a chain and a carboxyl group at the far end of the chain
questions.explanation: An α-amino acid is H₂N-CH(R)-COOH: both groups are on the α-carbon. The amino acids differ only in their side chain, R.

questions.stem: Which is the zwitterion form of the amino acid glycine, H₂NCH₂COOH?
questions.explanation: In a zwitterion the carboxyl group has donated its proton to the amino group, giving one positive and one negative charge on the same molecule. H₃N⁺CH₂COOH is the form found in strongly acidic solution.

questions.stem: Amino acids are crystalline solids with high melting points and are usually soluble in water. Why?
options: They have large non-polar side chains with strong dispersion forces
They are small molecules with only weak dipole-dipole forces
They exist as zwitterions, held together by strong ionic attractions
They form long covalent networks through peptide bonds in the solid
questions.explanation: In the solid, each zwitterion is attracted to its neighbours by forces between full positive and negative charges, much like an ionic lattice. These charges also interact strongly with polar water molecules. Peptide bonds only form when amino acids react with each other.

questions.stem: Glycine is dissolved in a strongly acidic solution at pH 1. In which form is it mainly present?
questions.explanation: At low pH there are many H⁺ ions, so the carboxylate group accepts a proton and the amino group stays protonated, giving an overall positive ion. In strongly basic solution the opposite happens, giving H₂NCH₂COO⁻.

questions.stem: How does a peptide bond form between two amino acids?
options: The COOH of one reacts with the NH₂ of the other, releasing water
The NH₂ groups of both amino acids react, releasing ammonia
The side chains react together, forming a covalent bridge
The COOH groups of both amino acids react, releasing water
questions.explanation: A peptide (amide) bond, -CO-NH-, forms in a condensation reaction between the carboxyl group of one amino acid and the amino group of another. Covalent bridges between side chains, such as disulfide bridges, are part of tertiary structure.

questions.stem: Glycine and alanine react to form dipeptides. How many different dipeptides containing one of each amino acid are possible?
questions.explanation: The free amino group can be on either amino acid, so glycine-alanine and alanine-glycine are different molecules with different sequences. Dipeptides made from two glycines or two alanines are not counted, since each must contain one of each.

questions.stem: What is the primary structure of a protein?
options: The coiling of the chain into an α-helix
The overall three-dimensional folded shape of the chain
The hydrogen bonds between adjacent chains
The sequence of amino acids in the polypeptide chain
questions.explanation: The primary structure is the order of amino acids, held together by covalent peptide bonds. Helices and sheets are secondary structure, and the overall folded shape is tertiary structure.

questions.stem: Which interaction produces the α-helix and β-pleated sheet structures in proteins?
options: Dispersion forces between non-polar side chains of the chain
Hydrogen bonds between C=O and N-H groups of the peptide backbone
Disulfide bridges between cysteine side chains in the chain
Ionic attractions between oppositely charged side chains
questions.explanation: Secondary structure comes from hydrogen bonding between the amide N-H and carbonyl C=O groups of the backbone: within one chain for an α-helix, and between adjacent chains for a β-pleated sheet. Interactions between side chains produce tertiary structure.

questions.stem: How does the hydrogen bonding in a β-pleated sheet differ from that in an α-helix?
options: In a sheet it is between adjacent chains; in a helix it is within one chain
In a sheet it is within one chain; in a helix it is between adjacent chains
In a sheet it is between side chains; in a helix it is between backbones
In a sheet it is ionic; in a helix it is between C=O and N-H groups
questions.explanation: Both structures are held by hydrogen bonds between C=O and N-H groups of the backbone. In an α-helix these link groups along the same coiled chain; in a β-pleated sheet they link neighbouring polypeptide chains lying side by side.

questions.stem: Which type of bond holds the amino acids together in the primary structure of a protein?
questions.explanation: The primary structure is the covalently bonded chain of amino acids joined by peptide (amide) bonds. Hydrogen bonds, ionic interactions and disulfide bridges hold the chain in its secondary and tertiary shapes.

questions.stem: Two cysteine residues, each with the side chain -CH₂SH, lie close together in a folded protein. Which interaction can form between them?
options: A peptide bond between the side chains
Dispersion forces only, as S-H is non-polar
questions.explanation: The two -SH groups can be oxidised to form a covalent S-S bond, a disulfide bridge, which strongly holds the tertiary structure in place. Peptide bonds join the backbone, not side chains.

questions.stem: In a folded protein, a lysine side chain, -(CH₂)₄NH₃⁺, lies next to an aspartate side chain, -CH₂COO⁻. Which interaction holds them together?
questions.explanation: The side chains carry opposite full charges, so they attract each other in an ionic interaction (a salt bridge), which contributes to the tertiary structure. Disulfide bridges form only between cysteine side chains.

questions.stem: Valine and leucine have non-polar hydrocarbon side chains. Which interaction mainly occurs between these side chains in a folded protein?
questions.explanation: Non-polar side chains can only attract each other through dispersion forces. They tend to cluster together inside the folded protein, away from water.

questions.stem: Serine has the side chain -CH₂OH. Which interaction can two serine side chains form in a folded protein?
options: A hydrogen bond between the O-H groups
A disulfide bridge between the oxygens
A peptide bond between the side chains
questions.explanation: The O-H group of one serine side chain can hydrogen bond to the oxygen of another. Serine side chains are uncharged, so they cannot form ionic interactions, and disulfide bridges need sulfur.

questions.stem: A protein is gently heated, and it loses its folded shape and its function. Which level of structure remains intact?
questions.explanation: Gentle heating disrupts the hydrogen bonds, ionic interactions and dispersion forces that hold the secondary and tertiary structure. The covalent peptide bonds of the primary structure need far more energy to break, so the amino acid sequence remains.

questions.stem: What is the Protein Data Bank?
options: A laboratory that makes synthetic proteins for medicines and sells them
A database of amino acid prices used by the food and medicine industries
An international repository of protein structure data used by scientists worldwide
A national register that sets the safe levels of protein in Australian foods
questions.explanation: The Protein Data Bank stores structural data for proteins, contributed to and used by scientists around the world. Knowing a protein's structure helps explain its function, because the two are closely linked.
